Part 1
Big ideas about computing
These hold whether you're using Word, Obsidian, Excel, or an AI agent.
Big idea 1 · built from the bottom up
The layers of a computer
You (and agents)
Act through programs. Claude is one of them.
Programs
Word, Chrome, Obsidian, Terminal: open and save files.
Files
Named bundles of data: syllabus.docx, photo.png
Directories (folders)
A tree of folders. A file's address is its path.
Operating system
macOS, Windows: keeps the tree, runs programs, sets access.
Hardware
Processor, memory, and the drive that stores the bytes.
Most apps hide the two middle layers. Today we look at them directly.

Every file lives at an address in a tree
/
└── Users/
└── you/
├── Desktop/

└── GAIW/

A folder holds files and other folders. That nesting makes a tree.
Follow the gold route from the top. Written out, that route is the file's path:
/Users/you/Documents/GAIW/syllabus.docx
Windows: C:\Users\you\Documents\GAIW\syllabus.docx

Big idea 7 · a feedback loop
Outputs become inputs
Claude writes a note today. Tomorrow's run reads it.
What a system produces shapes what it does next.
"Every output is a potential input."
Input
Process
Output
the output becomes the next input
Big idea 8 · since Week 1
Generative and deterministic, together
Generative
A language model drafts and proposes. Flexible, but it varies run to run.
Deterministic
An ordinary program counts and checks. Same input, same output.
Prompt
Many possible outputs
Run it again: a different path.
Input
Fixed steps
Same output
Run it again: the identical result.
Big idea 9
Automation is a trigger, a script and a log
Trigger
7am, or a new file arrives
Script
A fixed list of steps, nobody watching
Log
One line per run
log.md
Mon 7:00 ran · 3 new notes
Tue 7:00 ran · 2 new notes
Wed 7:00 (no line)
Thu 7:00 ran · 4 new notes
Wednesday's run failed, and nothing announced it. A missing line is the only alarm.
Big idea 10
Where code runs decides what it can reach
Your computer
can install software
A sandbox
a walled-off space
The cloud
always on, somewhere else
direct, with your permission
stops at the wall: only what you hand it
only while connected
Your files
Before "can it do this?", ask "where is it running?"
Part 2
An auto-updating research database
The same ten ideas, inside one thing we build today with Claude and Obsidian.
About the name
The internet calls this a "second brain." We don't.
A folder of files doesn't remember, understand, or care whether anything in it is true.
It stores text. A program rearranges that text when something triggers it.
Question
What does "second brain" lead you to expect that this folder can't do?

In the database
CLAUDE.md: the rules are a file
CLAUDE.md is a text file in the folder. Claude reads it at the start of every run and follows it.
Change one line, run again, and compare. Same "one variable" move as Domer Dogs.
## Rules
- Never invent a source or date.
- If two sources disagree, link both.
- Never edit raw/ or insights/.
- Describe software plainly; not as
thinking, knowing or remembering.

Step 1 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Code tab
Install Obsidian and make your folder
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: get the Obsidian app working on this computer so I can look at a research database I'm about to build. I've never installed software this way. Work out what kind of computer I have, tell me your plan in plain words, install Obsidian from its official source only, and check that it worked. Then make a folder called GAIW Research Database in my Documents.
You're done when: Claude tells you Obsidian's version number and the Obsidian window opens.
Step 1, continued
Who: Claude or you
Where: Code tab
What you'll see, and the by-hand way
What you'll see
Claude tells you its plan, then stops before every command and asks permission. Read its explanation, then choose Allow. Windows may ask "Do you want to allow this app to make changes?" Choose Yes. The first time Obsidian opens, a Mac may say it was downloaded from the internet. Choose Open.
If the install doesn't work
  1. Go to obsidian.md and click Download. The site picks Mac or Windows for you.
  2. Mac: open the downloaded .dmg file, drag the Obsidian icon onto the Applications folder, then eject the disk image. Windows: run the downloaded .exe and accept the defaults.
  3. Open Obsidian from Applications (Mac) or the Start menu (Windows). Choose Open if your computer asks whether you're sure.
  4. Make an empty folder called GAIW Research Database in your Documents folder.
Step 2 of 11
Who: You
Where: Cowork
Connect your folder to Cowork
You do this
Start a new Cowork task and add the folder Documents → GAIW Research Database. Cowork can now read and write in that folder and nowhere else on your computer.
Step 3 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Plan and build the database
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: turn this folder into a research database on my State of the Field topic that updates itself and that I can explore in Obsidian. Before you build anything, interview me: ask a few questions about my topic and how I'll use it. Then propose how to organize it (original sources kept untouched, a note per source, a note per idea, a list of everything, a log) and the rules you'll follow, written in CLAUDE.md. One rule is mine: insights/ is where I write, and you never do. Wait for my OK before you build.
You're done when: Claude has asked about your topic, shown you a plan, and built the folders after you said OK.
Step 4 of 11
Who: Claude, then you
Where: Cowork
Turn "Keeping Up" into rules
First, you: Open "Some Ways to Keep Up" (also in the Week 2 row of the syllabus). Choose File → Download → PDF, and move the PDF into your GAIW Research Database/raw/ folder.
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: your rules for finding and judging sources should follow this course's advice. The handout "Some Ways to Keep Up" is in raw/. Read it, tell me its main points in your own words, and ask me which I agree with and where I already go to follow my topic. Then draft sourcing rules into CLAUDE.md and show me what you changed.
Then you: Read Claude's draft. Delete anything you disagree with, and replace the general list with people, newsletters and sites that cover your own topic. These are your rules now.
Step 5 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Color the graph
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: when I open Obsidian's graph, I want to see at a glance which dots are sources, which are ideas, which are my insights and which are system files. Set that up, and tell me where to look.
You're done when: The graph shows four colors.
Step 6 of 11
Who: You
Where: Obsidian
Open your folder in Obsidian
You do this
In Obsidian's start window, choose Open folder as vault, click Open, and pick Documents → GAIW Research Database. Nothing gets imported; Obsidian just shows the files that are already in the folder.

Step 7 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Add five real sources
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: start filling the database with real, recent sources on my topic, following the rules in CLAUDE.md. Show me five candidates and why each one passes the rules before you add anything. After I agree, write the notes, link them to the ideas they support, and log what you did. Never invent a source.
Then you: Open two of the new source notes and click their links. Does each source exist, and does the note describe it correctly?
Step 8 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Make a table and a map
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: two more ways to look at what's here: a table of my sources I can sort, and a map of how my ideas connect. Make them as files Obsidian can open, and tell me where to click.
You're done when: You open the table and the map in Obsidian where Claude told you to click.
Step 9 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Run a check-up
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: to trust this database. Give it a check-up: broken links, notes nothing points to, sources missing key details, notes the index leaves out. Do the counting with a small script so the numbers are exact, fix what you can, write a short report, and tell me what you couldn't fix.
You're done when: Claude's report says everything passed, or tells you exactly what it couldn't fix. You install nothing; Claude runs the script itself.
Step 10 of 11
Who: Claude
Where: Cowork
Schedule it
Tell Claude your goal
My goal: this database keeps itself current every weekday morning without me. Set up a scheduled task that looks for new developments using CLAUDE.md, runs the check-up, and logs what happened. Ask me what time works, and show me the task when it's set.
You're done when: The task appears in your list of scheduled tasks.
Step 11 of 11
Who: You
Where: Obsidian
Write one insight
You do this
Make a new note in insights/. Claude never writes here. Write three things: a claim you now believe about your topic; the notes that convinced you, linked by typing their names in double brackets, like [[Note name]]; and what evidence would change your mind. Then open the graph view and find your green node.
